column1: 00 TRIAGE · Your 1000 to 1300 math target
column2: You need roughly 2 out of 3 math questions right, NOT all of them. | Plan: get 100% of Easy, most Medium, and deliberately guess-and-move on Hard. | Every card tagged E is non-negotiable. M is where your points are. H is labeled SKIP-OK when it is a known time sink.

column1: 00 TRIAGE · Where the questions actually come from
column2: Of 1,925 SAT math items in College Board's bank: Algebra 616, Advanced Math 540, Problem-Solving/Data 421, Geometry/Trig 348. | Algebra is the most Easy-weighted domain (269 Easy). Circles and Right-Triangle Trig are the most Hard-weighted (only 12 Easy between them). | Study in that order.

column1: 00 TRIAGE · The 3-second decision
column2: Read the question. If you do not know your first move within ~10 seconds, flag it and go. | At your level a guessed Hard question costs you nothing; a rushed Easy question costs you a point you already owned. | Finish all Easy/Medium first, then come back.

column1: 00 TRIAGE · When to NOT use Desmos
column2: Desmos is slower than your head for: simple percent of a number, unit conversion, one-step solving, mean of 4 small numbers. | Use Desmos when there are variables on both sides, ugly decimals, a system, a quadratic, or a table of data.

column1: 01 DESMOS · The single highest-value move
column2: Any equation of the form f(x) = g(x): type y = (left side) on line 1 and y = (right side) on line 2, then click the gray intersection dot. | The x-coordinate is the solution. | This replaces almost all algebra on the test.

column1: 01 DESMOS · Universal rewrite (cleaner than two graphs)
column2: For f(x) = g(x), instead graph y = (left side) - (right side) on ONE line and click the x-intercept. | Same answer, half the clutter, and it makes 'how many solutions' obvious at a glance.

column1: 01 DESMOS · Gray dots are the whole game
column2: Desmos marks every intersection, x-intercept, y-intercept, vertex, min and max with a clickable gray dot. | Click it and it prints the exact coordinates. | You almost never need to compute a vertex or root by hand.

column1: 01 DESMOS · Sliders appear automatically
column2: Type any letter that is not x or y (like y = kx + 3) and Desmos offers 'add slider'. | Drag k and watch the graph. | This solves every 'for what value of the constant...' question without algebra.

column1: 01 DESMOS · Table back-solving
column2: Ctrl+Alt+T opens a table. Put the four answer choices in the x1 column, type the question's expression in the y1 header. | Desmos evaluates all four at once. | Best move for 'which value satisfies' when the algebra is ugly.

column1: 01 DESMOS · Statistics in one line
column2: Type L = [12, 7, 5, 15, 9] then mean(L), median(L), stdev(L), total(L). | Works for any list question. | Faster and safer than adding by hand under time pressure.

column1: 01 DESMOS · Parentheses discipline
column2: Always wrap numerators, denominators and bases: (3x+2)/(x-4), (x-1)^2, 2^(x+1). | The most common Desmos error is a silently mistyped expression, not a wrong method.

column1: 01 DESMOS · Degree mode before ANY trig
column2: Open the wrench (graph settings) and switch to Degrees before touching a trig question. | Desmos defaults to radians. | This single setting causes more wrong trig answers than the math itself.

column1: 01 DESMOS · Zoom before you trust a coordinate
column2: If you are reading a value off the graph, zoom in on the dot first. | Pinch/scroll until the coordinate is unambiguous. | A badly scaled window hides vertices, intercepts and second intersections.

column1: 01 DESMOS · Function notation works directly
column2: Type f(x) = 2x^2 - 3x + 1 on one line, then type f(4) on the next and Desmos prints the value. | Also handles composition: f(g(2)). | Use this for every 'what is f(...)' question instead of substituting by hand.

column1: 02 LIN-1VAR · E · 'If 8x = 6, what is the value of 72x?'
column2: SIGNAL: they give you one equation and ask for a MULTIPLE of the variable, not the variable. | MOVE: do not solve for x. Notice 72x is 9 times 8x, so the answer is 9 x 6 = 54. | TRAP: solving for x = 0.75 then multiplying works too but wastes 20 seconds and invites a decimal error.

column1: 02 LIN-1VAR · E · 'If x/8 = 5, what is the value of 8x?'
column2: SIGNAL: fraction on the left, asks for a scaled version. | MOVE: x = 40, so 8x = 320. | TRAP: the mirror-image answer 8x = 5 x 8 = 40 is always a choice. Solve for x first, then scale.

column1: 02 LIN-1VAR · E · 'Which equation has the same solution as the given equation?'
column2: SIGNAL: asks for an EQUIVALENT equation, not a value. | DESMOS: solve the original (graph both sides, click intersection) to get x. Then test each choice by plugging that x in. | Faster: look for a choice that is the original times a constant or with terms moved.

column1: 02 LIN-1VAR · E · Perimeter or total-cost sentence with one unknown
column2: SIGNAL: a real-world sentence, one thing you do not know, the word 'total' or 'perimeter'. | MOVE: write total = sum of parts, then solve. Isosceles perimeter 83 with two sides of 24: third = 83 - 48 = 35. | TRAP: 'each of the two congruent sides' means subtract 24 twice, not once.

column1: 02 LIN-1VAR · M · Variables on BOTH sides
column2: SIGNAL: x appears left and right, often with parentheses and fractions. | DESMOS: y = left side, y = right side, click intersection. Read the x-value. | This is the cleanest 15 seconds on the test. Do not distribute by hand.

column1: 02 LIN-1VAR · M · 'The equation has no solution. What is the value of a?'
column2: SIGNAL: 'no solution' plus an unknown coefficient. | RULE: no solution means same slope, different intercept (parallel lines). Set the x-coefficients equal and solve for the constant. | DESMOS: put a slider on a and drag until the two lines become parallel and separate.

column1: 02 LIN-1VAR · M · 'The equation is true for all values of x'
column2: SIGNAL: 'all values of x', 'infinitely many solutions', or 'identity'. | RULE: both sides must be identical. Match x-coefficients AND match constants. | DESMOS: slider the unknown until the two graphs sit exactly on top of each other.

column1: 02 LIN-1VAR · H · Equation with the unknown inside a denominator
column2: SIGNAL: x in the bottom of a fraction. | DESMOS: graph both sides and click the intersection. | TRAP: any x that makes a denominator zero is NOT a solution even if it appears algebraically. Desmos shows this as a hole or asymptote, so check the graph.

column1: 03 LIN-FUNC · E · 'f has slope 3 and passes through (0, -8). Which equation defines f?'
column2: SIGNAL: slope plus a point whose x is 0. | MOVE: (0, b) IS the y-intercept, so write y = 3x - 8 immediately. | TRAP: only skip the point-slope work when the x-coordinate is 0. Otherwise use y - y1 = m(x - x1).

column1: 03 LIN-FUNC · E · 'h(0) = 41 and h(1) = 40. Which equation defines h?'
column2: SIGNAL: two function values one step apart. | MOVE: h(0) = 41 is the intercept; the drop from 41 to 40 is the slope, so m = -1. Answer y = -x + 41. | This exact setup appears constantly. Learn to read h(0) as 'b'.

column1: 03 LIN-FUNC · E · 'The function f is defined by f(x) = 0.7x + 55. What is f(20)?'
column2: SIGNAL: a clean 'evaluate the function' ask. | DESMOS: type f(x) = 0.7x + 55, then type f(20). It prints 69. | TRAP: do not mix up f(20) (plug in 20) with 'f(x) = 20' (solve for x). Read which one they want.

column1: 03 LIN-FUNC · E · Table of values, asks for the linear equation
column2: SIGNAL: a small table of x and y, answer choices are equations. | MOVE: slope = change in y over change in x between any two rows. Then find b. | DESMOS: Ctrl+Alt+T, enter the points, then type y1 ~ mx1 + b to get slope and intercept exactly.

column1: 03 LIN-FUNC · E · Graph shown, asks for slope or intercept
column2: SIGNAL: a pictured line with two labeled points. | MOVE: slope = rise over run using the two labeled points; the y-intercept is where it crosses the vertical axis. | TRAP: read the axis scale. Gridlines are often worth 2 or 5, not 1.

column1: 03 LIN-FUNC · M · Interpret the slope in context
column2: SIGNAL: 'what does 0.7 represent in this context?' | RULE: the slope is always 'units of y per ONE unit of x'. Say it in the problem's own words. | TRAP: the intercept is the starting/initial value; the slope is the rate of change. Half the wrong answers swap these two.

column1: 03 LIN-FUNC · M · Interpret the y-intercept in context
column2: SIGNAL: 'what does 55 represent?' | RULE: the value of y when x = 0, i.e. the initial, starting, base, or fixed amount. | Phrase it as 'the ___ when no ___ have occurred'.

column1: 03 LIN-FUNC · M · Two conditions, find the function, then evaluate
column2: SIGNAL: two points given in words, then asked for a third value. | DESMOS: put both points in a table, run y1 ~ mx1 + b, then evaluate the fitted line at the value they want. | Avoids two separate chances at an arithmetic slip.

column1: 03 LIN-FUNC · H · Function transformations (f(x) + k, f(x + k), -f(x))
column2: SIGNAL: a new function defined in terms of f. | RULES: +k outside shifts UP; +k inside shifts LEFT (opposite of what it looks like); a negative outside flips vertically. | DESMOS: graph f and the transformed version together and just look.

column1: 04 LIN-2VAR · E · 'A line has slope -1/2 and passes through (0, 3). Which equation represents it?'
column2: SIGNAL: slope plus the y-intercept point. | MOVE: y = -x/2 + 3, done. | DESMOS check: graph your choice and confirm it passes through the given point.

column1: 04 LIN-2VAR · E · 'The y-intercept of 12x + 2y = 18 is (0, y). What is y?'
column2: SIGNAL: standard form, asks for an intercept. | MOVE: set x = 0 and solve: 2y = 18, y = 9. | DESMOS: just graph 12x + 2y = 18 as typed (Desmos accepts standard form) and click the y-intercept dot.

column1: 04 LIN-2VAR · E · 'Which table gives three values of x and their y for y = -4x + 40?'
column2: SIGNAL: answer choices are TABLES. | MOVE: test ONE easy row from each choice, usually x = 0 or x = 1. Eliminate on the first mismatch. | Do not verify all three rows of a choice before moving on.

column1: 04 LIN-2VAR · E · '46 = 2a + 2b. If a = 9, what is b?'
column2: SIGNAL: a formula with two letters, one value supplied. | MOVE: substitute and solve: 46 = 18 + 2b, b = 14. | TRAP: read which letter they gave you. Swapping a and b is the intended error.

column1: 04 LIN-2VAR · M · Parallel and perpendicular slopes
column2: RULES: parallel means EQUAL slopes. Perpendicular means slopes multiply to -1 (flip the fraction and change the sign). | Perpendicular to slope 2/3 is -3/2. | TRAP: 'negative reciprocal' means BOTH flip and negate, not just one.

column1: 04 LIN-2VAR · M · Convert standard form to slope-intercept
column2: SIGNAL: Ax + By = C but the answer choices are y = mx + b. | SHORTCUT: slope = -A/B and y-intercept = C/B. | For 12x + 2y = 18: slope -6, intercept 9. Memorize this; it saves rearranging.

column1: 04 LIN-2VAR · M · Two points given, find the equation
column2: MOVE: slope = (y2 - y1)/(x2 - x1), then plug one point in to get b. | DESMOS: table with the two points, then y1 ~ mx1 + b. | TRAP: keep the subtraction order consistent in numerator and denominator.

column1: 04 LIN-2VAR · H · 'x-intercept of the graph is (a, 0). What is a?'
column2: SIGNAL: asks for an intercept expressed with a letter. | MOVE: set y = 0 and solve for x. | DESMOS: graph it and click the x-intercept dot. | TRAP: x-intercept means y = 0. Students reflexively set x = 0. Slow down on this one.

column1: 05 SYSTEMS · E · 'The solution to the system is (x, y). What is the value of y?'
column2: SIGNAL: two linear equations stacked, asks for ONE coordinate. | DESMOS: type each equation on its own line exactly as printed, click the gray intersection dot, read the coordinate they asked for. | TRAP: they ask for y, or x, or x + y, or 2y. Re-read the final line before you bubble.

column1: 05 SYSTEMS · E · One equation is already solved (x = 8, or y = 4)
column2: SIGNAL: one line gives a variable outright. | MOVE: substitute mentally into the other equation. x = 8 with x + 3y = 26 gives 3y = 18, y = 6. | Faster than Desmos here, but Desmos still works if you are unsure.

column1: 05 SYSTEMS · E · 'What is the value of x + y?'
column2: SIGNAL: asks for a COMBINATION of the two unknowns. | MOVE: find the intersection in Desmos, then add the coordinates. | SHORTCUT: sometimes adding the two equations directly produces x + y in one step. Check for that before graphing.

column1: 05 SYSTEMS · M · Both equations messy, ugly coefficients or decimals
column2: DESMOS: type both lines as printed, no rearranging. Click the intersection. | This is the single best return on Desmos on the whole test. | Avoid doing elimination by hand at your score level; it is mostly error surface.

column1: 05 SYSTEMS · M · 'The system has NO solution. Find the constant.'
column2: RULE: no solution means the lines are PARALLEL: equal slopes, different y-intercepts. | MOVE: set the slopes equal and solve for the unknown. | DESMOS: slider the constant and drag until the lines are parallel and clearly separate.

column1: 05 SYSTEMS · M · 'The system has INFINITELY many solutions.'
column2: RULE: infinitely many means the two equations are the SAME line. One is a constant multiple of the other. | MOVE: find the multiplier that maps one equation onto the other, then match the remaining coefficient. | DESMOS: slider until one graph disappears into the other.

column1: 05 SYSTEMS · M · 'Exactly one solution' with an unknown constant
column2: RULE: exactly one solution means the slopes are DIFFERENT. | So find the value that would make them parallel, and the answer is every value except that one. | Read whether they want the excluded value or the allowed range.

column1: 05 SYSTEMS · H · Answer choices contain a letter like r or 3 - 3r
column2: SIGNAL: the choices are expressions in a parameter, not numbers. | HEURISTIC: this almost always means the system has infinitely many solutions, i.e. the lines coincide. | Set up the proportionality of all three coefficients and solve.

column1: 05 SYSTEMS · H · System given as a GRAPH plus one equation
column2: SIGNAL: a pictured line and a printed equation. | MOVE: read two clean lattice points off the picture to get the drawn line's equation, then intersect with the printed one in Desmos. | TRAP: check the axis scale before reading points.

column1: 06 SYS-WORD · E · Two items, two totals (count and money)
column2: SIGNAL: 'x adult and y child tickets', a total COUNT and a total COST. | SETUP: one equation for the count (x + y = total) and one for the money (price1·x + price2·y = total cost). | DESMOS: type both, click intersection.

column1: 06 SYS-WORD · E · 'Total of 364 straws made triangles and rectangles'
column2: SIGNAL: a total of PARTS distributed between two shapes/objects with different per-unit counts. | SETUP: 3t + 4r = 364 for the pieces, plus whatever second fact they give (often total number of polygons). | TRAP: use sides per shape (3 and 4), not the number of shapes.

column1: 06 SYS-WORD · M · Translating the words into two equations
column2: CHECKLIST: define both variables in writing. One equation counts THINGS, the other counts VALUE (dollars, grams, minutes, points). | 'twice as many a as b' is a = 2b, not 2a = b. Say it out loud to catch the flip.

column1: 06 SYS-WORD · M · 'How many more x than y?'
column2: SIGNAL: asks for a DIFFERENCE, not a value. | MOVE: solve the system in Desmos, then subtract. | TRAP: this is the most common careless-error question in the section. The intersection is not the answer; the difference is.

column1: 06 SYS-WORD · M · Mixture, rate, or 'combined' problems
column2: SETUP: one equation for total AMOUNT, one for total CONCENTRATION or total RATE. | Example: x + y = 10 liters and 0.2x + 0.5y = 0.3(10). | DESMOS: type both and intersect. Do not clear the decimals by hand.

column1: 06 SYS-WORD · H · Word problem where the question asks for the constant
column2: SIGNAL: a scenario plus 'for what value of k would there be no solution / one solution'. | MOVE: translate to two equations first, then apply the parallel/identical-line rules. | The wording is harder than the math; the math is still just slopes.

column1: 07 INEQ · E · 'Minimum rate was 0.6 and maximum was 1.8. Which inequality is true?'
column2: SIGNAL: the words minimum and maximum, answer choices are inequalities. | MOVE: minimum means 'greater than or equal to', maximum means 'less than or equal to'. So 0.6 <= r <= 1.8. | TRAP: 'at least' and 'no less than' both mean >=.

column1: 07 INEQ · E · 'The point (8, 2) is a solution to which system of inequalities?'
column2: SIGNAL: a specific point, answer choices are inequality systems. | MOVE: plug the point into each choice and check BOTH inequalities hold. Eliminate on the first failure. | Pure arithmetic; no graphing needed.

column1: 07 INEQ · M · 'For which table are all values solutions to the inequality?'
column2: SIGNAL: an inequality plus answer choices that are tables. | DESMOS: graph the inequality (it shades). Then plot the table's points and see which set lands entirely inside the shading. | TRAP: ALL rows must satisfy it, so one bad row kills the choice.

column1: 07 INEQ · M · Translating constraint words
column2: DICTIONARY: 'at least' >=, 'at most' <=, 'no more than' <=, 'more than' >, 'fewer than' <, 'minimum' >=, 'maximum' <=. | 'At least 100 centimeters' is h >= 100, strictly. | Most inequality errors are vocabulary errors, not math errors.

column1: 07 INEQ · M · Systems of inequalities, find the feasible region
column2: DESMOS: type each inequality on its own line using > or <. Desmos shades automatically; the answer lives in the overlap. | Then test which listed point sits in the doubly-shaded area.

column1: 07 INEQ · H · Inequality with an unknown coefficient
column2: SIGNAL: a slider-shaped question, 'for what values of a is the point a solution'. | DESMOS: slider on a, watch the shaded region move across the point. | Note the boundary value, then decide whether it is included (solid) or excluded (dashed).

column1: 08 EQUIV · E · 'Which expression is equivalent to 34x + 34y?'
column2: SIGNAL: 'equivalent to', simple common factor. | MOVE: factor it: 34(x + y). | DESMOS CHECK: for single-variable versions, graph the original and your choice; if the curves sit exactly on top of each other, they are equivalent.

column1: 08 EQUIV · E · 'Which expression is equivalent to 256w^2 - 676?'
column2: SIGNAL: something squared MINUS something squared. | RULE: difference of squares, a^2 - b^2 = (a - b)(a + b). Here (16w - 26)(16w + 26). | Recognizing 256 = 16^2 and 676 = 26^2 is the whole question.

column1: 08 EQUIV · E · 'Which expression is equivalent to 5x^5 - 6x^4 + 8x^3?'
column2: SIGNAL: every term shares a power of x. | MOVE: pull out the LOWEST power: x^3(5x^2 - 6x + 8). | TRAP: factoring out x^5 instead of x^3 produces negative exponents and a wrong choice that is offered.

column1: 08 EQUIV · M · The overlap-graph trick for 'equivalent'
column2: DESMOS: graph the original expression as y = (original) and each answer choice as y = (choice). | The equivalent one lies perfectly on top and the others visibly separate. | This works even when you cannot do the algebra at all. Highest-value move in this section.

column1: 08 EQUIV · M · Factoring a quadratic ax^2 + bx + c
column2: MOVE: find two numbers that multiply to a·c and add to b, then split and factor. | FASTER: graph y = the quadratic, click the two x-intercepts at r and s, and the factorization is a(x - r)(x - s). | Lean on the graph, which will not slip on a sign the way hand-factoring can.

column1: 08 EQUIV · M · Adding or subtracting rational expressions
column2: MOVE: common denominator, combine numerators, then simplify. | DESMOS CHECK: graph original and answer; overlapping curves confirm it. | TRAP: distribute the minus sign across the ENTIRE second numerator.

column1: 08 EQUIV · H · 'Can be rewritten as a(4x^2 + 7x + 13). What is a?'
column2: SIGNAL: a scaled version of a given expression, solve for the scale factor. | MOVE: divide any single matching coefficient. 0.36 / 4 = 0.09, and check 0.63 / 7 = 0.09 and 1.17 / 13 = 0.09. | Confirm with a second coefficient; that is your error check.

column1: 08 EQUIV · H · Exponent rules you must have cold
column2: x^a · x^b = x^(a+b). x^a / x^b = x^(a-b). (x^a)^b = x^(ab). x^0 = 1. x^(-a) = 1/x^a. | x^(1/2) = sqrt(x), and x^(m/n) is the n-th root of x^m. | These appear as 'equivalent expression' choices constantly.

column1: 09 NONLIN-EQ · E · '8x^2 - 40 = 32. What is the POSITIVE solution?'
column2: SIGNAL: a squared term and the word positive (or negative). | MOVE: isolate, then square-root: x^2 = 9, x = 3 or -3, take +3. | DESMOS: graph y = 8x^2 - 40 and y = 32, click the right-hand intersection. | TRAP: forgetting that squaring gives TWO roots.

column1: 09 NONLIN-EQ · E · 'k^2 - 53 = 91. What is the positive solution?'
column2: MOVE: k^2 = 144, k = 12. | DESMOS if the numbers are not clean squares. | Always check which root they asked for before bubbling.

column1: 09 NONLIN-EQ · E · '6r = 7s + t. Express s in terms of r and t.'
column2: SIGNAL: 'in terms of', rearrange a formula. | MOVE: isolate the requested letter: s = (6r - t)/7. | TRAP: the choices include (6r + t)/7 and 6r/7 - t. Move terms one at a time and keep the division over the WHOLE numerator.

column1: 09 NONLIN-EQ · E · Equation with x inside a fraction, like 1/(x+8) = 1/(6+8)
column2: SIGNAL: identical structure on both sides. | MOVE: if the forms match, match the insides: x + 8 = 14, so x = 6. | DESMOS backup: graph both sides and intersect.

column1: 09 NONLIN-EQ · M · Mixed system: one line and one curve
column2: SIGNAL: a linear equation stacked with a quadratic or exponential. | DESMOS: type both, click the intersection(s). | KEY: a line and a parabola can meet at 0, 1, or 2 points, so read whether they want a specific one ('positive', 'greater', 'in quadrant I').

column1: 09 NONLIN-EQ · M · 'At what point (x, y) do the graphs intersect?'
column2: SIGNAL: asks for the full ordered pair. | DESMOS: type both equations, click the dot, read both coordinates. | TRAP: if there are two intersections, use the extra condition in the question to pick the right one.

column1: 09 NONLIN-EQ · M · Radical equations (square root of an expression)
column2: MOVE: isolate the radical, square both sides, solve. | MUST DO: plug answers back in. Squaring creates extraneous solutions that are not real answers. | DESMOS avoids this entirely: graph both sides and only real intersections show up.

column1: 09 NONLIN-EQ · M · The quadratic formula and the discriminant
column2: x = (-b ± sqrt(b^2 - 4ac)) / (2a). | DISCRIMINANT b^2 - 4ac: positive means 2 real solutions, zero means exactly 1, negative means none. | 'How many real solutions' questions are answered by the discriminant's sign alone.

column1: 09 NONLIN-EQ · H · 'Exactly one solution' for a line and a parabola
column2: MEANING: the line is TANGENT to the curve. | ALGEBRA: set them equal and force the discriminant to 0. | DESMOS: put a slider on the constant and drag until the two graphs just touch at a single point. Read the slider value.

column1: 09 NONLIN-EQ · H · SKIP-OK · Systems with two unknown constants
column2: SIGNAL: two letters to determine and heavy symbolic manipulation. | At a 1300 target this is a flag-and-guess question. | If you have time: slider both constants, or substitute the given point to generate two equations in the constants.

column1: 10 QUAD · E · 'What is the y-intercept of the graph?'
column2: MOVE: set x = 0, or just click the y-intercept dot in Desmos. | For g(x) = 11·(1/12)^x, g(0) = 11 because anything to the power 0 is 1. | TRAP: the base is not the intercept; the coefficient in front is.

column1: 10 QUAD · E · Graph shown with a labeled minimum or maximum
column2: SIGNAL: a pictured parabola with a turning point. | READ: the turning point IS the vertex (h, k). Minimum means the parabola opens up (a > 0); maximum means it opens down (a < 0). | Match to the vertex-form choice a(x - h)^2 + k.

column1: 10 QUAD · E · The three quadratic forms and what each one hands you
column2: STANDARD y = ax^2 + bx + c gives the y-intercept c. | FACTORED y = a(x - r)(x - s) gives the roots r and s. | VERTEX y = a(x - h)^2 + k gives the vertex (h, k). | The question tells you which form to want by what it asks for.

column1: 10 QUAD · M · 'What is the vertex / minimum / maximum value?'
column2: DESMOS: graph it and click the turning-point dot. Done. | BY HAND: x of the vertex = -b/(2a), then plug in for the y-value. | TRAP: 'minimum VALUE' means the y-coordinate; 'where does the minimum occur' means the x-coordinate.

column1: 10 QUAD · M · 'What are the zeros / roots / x-intercepts / solutions?'
column2: All four words mean the same thing: where y = 0. | DESMOS: graph and click the x-intercept dots. | TRAP: the roots of a(x - r)(x - s) are +r and +s, not -r and -s. The sign flips from what you see.

column1: 10 QUAD · M · Axis of symmetry and the midpoint shortcut
column2: The axis of symmetry is the vertical line x = -b/(2a), and it sits exactly halfway between the two roots. | So if the roots are 2 and 8, the vertex is at x = 5. | This shortcut answers many questions with no computation.

column1: 10 QUAD · M · Projectile word problem: 'maximum height at t seconds, hits ground at t seconds'
column2: SIGNAL: launched object, a max height, and a landing time. | READ IT AS: the vertex is (time of max, max height) and one root is the landing time. The other root is t = 0 (launch). | Match to vertex form or factored form accordingly.

column1: 10 QUAD · H · Completing the square to reach vertex form
column2: MOVE: factor out a, halve the x-coefficient, square it, add and subtract it inside. | FASTER: at a 1300 target, graph it in Desmos and click the vertex instead. | Keep this card for recognition only; do not spend study time drilling it.

column1: 10 QUAD · H · SKIP-OK · Symbolic quadratics with parameters
column2: SIGNAL: no numbers, just letters, asking about the nature of the roots. | This is a top-tier-score question. Flag it. | If forced: the discriminant's sign is nearly always the intended route.

column1: 11 GROWTH · E · The master exponential template
column2: y = A · b^(t/p) where A = starting amount, b = growth factor per period, p = length of one period. | Doubling: b = 2. Halving: b = 1/2. Tripling: b = 3. | 'Doubles every 10 years' from $890 gives M(t) = 890 · 2^(t/10).

column1: 11 GROWTH · E · Percent growth and decay factors
column2: GROWTH of r percent: multiply by (1 + r/100). A 7 percent increase means b = 1.07. | DECAY of r percent: multiply by (1 - r/100). A 7 percent decrease means b = 0.93. | TRAP: b = 1.07 is growth; b = 0.07 would be losing 93 percent.

column1: 11 GROWTH · E · Linear versus exponential: how to tell
column2: LINEAR adds the same AMOUNT each step (constant difference) and the words are 'per year', 'each month', 'increases by 5 units'. | EXPONENTIAL multiplies by the same FACTOR each step (constant ratio) and the words are 'percent', 'doubles', 'halves', 'per year compounded'. | Check a table by differencing, then by dividing.

column1: 11 GROWTH · M · Reading the period out of the exponent
column2: In A · b^(t/p), the p in the denominator is the time for ONE full multiplication. | 2^(t/10) doubles every 10 units; 2^(10t) doubles every 1/10 of a unit. | TRAP: t/10 versus 10t is the single most common exponential distractor pair.

column1: 11 GROWTH · M · Converting an annual rate to monthly
column2: Annual factor b over 12 months becomes b^(t/12) with t in months, or equivalently multiply the exponent. | For '3 percent per year over t months': 1.03^(t/12). | Read the units of t in the answer choices before choosing.

column1: 11 GROWTH · M · 'What does the 890 represent in M(t) = 890 · 2^(t/10)?'
column2: The coefficient in front is always the INITIAL or starting value (the value at t = 0). | The base tells you the growth behavior; the denominator in the exponent tells you the period. | These three interpretation questions repeat verbatim across tests.

column1: 11 GROWTH · H · Exponential given as a table, find the equation
column2: MOVE: divide consecutive y-values to get the common ratio b, and read A as the value at x = 0. | DESMOS: put the table in and run y1 ~ a·b^(x1). It returns a and b exactly. | Use regression; it beats hand-fitting every time.

column1: 12 RATES · E · 'Pits 12 pounds in 3 minutes. How long for 96 pounds?'
column2: SIGNAL: a rate plus a new quantity. | MOVE: set up one proportion, 12/3 = 96/x, cross-multiply: x = 24 minutes. | FASTER: 96 is 8 times 12, so 8 times 3 = 24 minutes. Look for the clean multiple first.

column1: 12 RATES · E · 'Spent $27 on oranges at $3 per pound. How many pounds?'
column2: SIGNAL: total divided by a per-unit price. | MOVE: 27 / 3 = 9 pounds. | TRAP: decide whether to multiply or divide by checking the units: dollars divided by dollars-per-pound leaves pounds.

column1: 12 RATES · E · Unit conversion with a given equivalence
column2: SIGNAL: they hand you '1 fathom = 6 feet'. | MOVE: multiply so the unwanted unit cancels: 58 fathoms x 6 feet/fathom = 348 feet. | TRAP: dividing instead of multiplying. Write the unit fraction so the old unit is on the bottom.

column1: 12 RATES · E · 'Completes 900 revolutions in 50 minutes. Revolutions per minute?'
column2: SIGNAL: the words 'per' in the answer's units. | MOVE: 'per' means divide: 900/50 = 18. | Whatever unit comes after 'per' goes in the denominator.

column1: 12 RATES · M · Two-step conversions (km/hr to m/s and similar)
column2: MOVE: chain the unit fractions so every unwanted unit cancels diagonally. | Write it out; do not do it mentally. | DESMOS: type the whole chain as one product and let it compute.

column1: 12 RATES · M · Scale factors and similar figures
column2: RULE: if lengths scale by k, AREAS scale by k^2 and VOLUMES scale by k^3. | Doubling every length multiplies area by 4 and volume by 8. | This is a favorite trap: they give a length ratio and ask for an area ratio.

column1: 12 RATES · M · Proportional relationship means y = kx
column2: SIGNAL: 'directly proportional', 'proportional relationship'. | MEANS: a straight line THROUGH THE ORIGIN, so y = kx with no constant term. | TRAP: y = kx + b is linear but NOT proportional. If the graph misses the origin, it is not proportional.

column1: 13 PCT · E · 'What is 23% of 100?' and 'What percentage of 300 is 75?'
column2: TRANSLATE: 'of' means multiply, 'is' means equals, 'what percent' means x/100. | 23% of 100 = 23. For the second: x/100 x 300 = 75, so x = 25. | Write the sentence as an equation before computing.

column1: 13 PCT · E · 'Of 250 trees, 6% are birch. How many birch?'
column2: MOVE: 0.06 x 250 = 15. | Convert the percent to a decimal first, then multiply. | TRAP: answers like 6 and 41.7 are offered for people who skip the conversion or divide.

column1: 13 PCT · E · 'Of 300,000 clips, 234,000 are large. What percentage?'
column2: MOVE: part over whole, then times 100: 234000/300000 = 0.78 = 78%. | TRAP: putting the whole on top. The word 'of' marks the whole.

column1: 13 PCT · M · Percent increase and decrease
column2: FORMULA: ((new - old)/old)·100. The denominator is ALWAYS the original. | TRAP: going 50 up then 50 down does not return you to the start. Compute sequentially with multipliers.

column1: 13 PCT · M · Successive percent changes
column2: MOVE: multiply the factors. Up 20% then down 10% is 1.20 x 0.90 = 1.08, a net 8% increase. | Never add or subtract the percentages. | This is the most reliably missed percent question.

column1: 13 PCT · M · 'After a 15% discount the price is $68. What was the original?'
column2: SIGNAL: they give you the AFTER value and want the BEFORE. | MOVE: divide, do not multiply: 68 / 0.85 = 80. | TRAP: taking 15% of 68 and adding it back gives the wrong answer. Set up 0.85x = 68.

column1: 13 PCT · H · Percent of a percent, and percent-point versus percent
column2: 'Rose from 20% to 25%' is a 5 PERCENTAGE-POINT rise but a 25 PERCENT increase. | Read carefully which one is asked. | The distinction is the entire question when it appears.

column1: 14 DATA-1 · E · Mean, median, mode, range definitions
column2: MEAN = sum / count. MEDIAN = middle value after SORTING. MODE = most frequent. RANGE = max - min. | DESMOS: L = [list], then mean(L), median(L), stdev(L). | TRAP: forgetting to sort before taking the median.

column1: 14 DATA-1 · E · Reading a bar graph or dot plot for a total or a count
column2: MOVE: read each bar's height off the axis and add only the ones asked about. | TRAP: check the axis increment (bars often step by 2, 5 or 10) and watch for a truncated axis that does not start at 0.

column1: 14 DATA-1 · E · Median from a frequency table or dot plot
column2: MOVE: find the total count n, then the median is at position (n+1)/2 counting up through the frequencies. | Do not average the frequencies; you are locating a position within them.

column1: 14 DATA-1 · M · Which measure changes when you add an outlier
column2: RULE: the MEAN and the RANGE and the standard deviation move a lot; the MEDIAN barely moves. | So 'resistant to outliers' always means median. | This exact comparison is asked repeatedly.

column1: 14 DATA-1 · M · Standard deviation by inspection (no computing)
column2: RULE: more SPREAD means larger standard deviation. Data clustered tightly around the center means smaller. | You are essentially never asked to compute it by hand; you compare two distributions by eye. | Same mean with wider spread = bigger SD.

column1: 14 DATA-1 · M · 'The mean of 9 integers is 42. Adding a 10th makes the mean 43. Find it.'
column2: MOVE: work with TOTALS, not means. Old total = 9 x 42 = 378. New total = 10 x 43 = 430. The new value is 430 - 378 = 52. | This total-based method solves every 'mean changes' question.

column1: 14 DATA-1 · H · Comparing two distributions in a two-part question
column2: MOVE: handle center (mean/median) and spread (range/SD) separately and state each one. | TRAP: a distribution can have the SAME mean and a very different spread, or vice versa. Do not let one drive your answer about the other.

column1: 15 DATA-2 · E · Reading a line of best fit off a scatterplot
column2: MOVE: read the y-value on the LINE at the requested x, not the nearest data point. | TRAP: 'predicted by the model' means use the line; 'actual' means use the dot. The difference between them is the residual.

column1: 15 DATA-2 · E · Identifying the shape of a scatterplot
column2: LINEAR looks like a straight trend. EXPONENTIAL curves upward with increasing steepness. QUADRATIC rises then falls (or vice versa). | Match the shape word to the equation family in the choices.

column1: 15 DATA-2 · M · Desmos regression: the single best move in this section
column2: MOVE: Ctrl+Alt+T for a table, enter the points, then type y1 ~ mx1 + b for linear, y1 ~ ax1^2 + bx1 + c for quadratic, y1 ~ ab^(x1) for exponential. | Desmos returns the exact coefficients plus R^2. | Higher R^2 means better fit, which settles 'which model' questions.

column1: 15 DATA-2 · M · Residuals
column2: RESIDUAL = actual minus predicted. Positive means the point sits ABOVE the line; negative means below. | A good model has residuals scattered randomly around zero with no pattern. | A curved residual pattern means you picked the wrong model family.

column1: 15 DATA-2 · M · Interpreting slope and intercept of a best-fit line
column2: Same as any linear function: slope is the predicted change in y per one unit of x; intercept is the predicted y at x = 0. | Say 'predicted' or 'on average' out loud. The right answer choice almost always includes that hedge.

column1: 15 DATA-2 · H · Correlation versus causation
column2: RULE: an observational study or a scatterplot can NEVER establish cause. Only a randomized controlled EXPERIMENT can. | The right answer is the cautious one: 'is associated with', 'there is a relationship'. | Be very wary of any choice containing 'causes' unless subjects were randomly assigned.

column1: 16 PROB · E · Probability from a one-way frequency table
column2: MOVE: favorable count over TOTAL count. 15 turkey out of 50 children is 15/50 = 0.3. | TRAP: make sure the denominator is the total the question names, not the table's grand total.

column1: 16 PROB · E · Probability from a two-way table
column2: MOVE: identify the row and column the question restricts you to, then read the right cell over the right total. | Underline the group named in the question before you look at the table.

column1: 16 PROB · M · Conditional probability: 'GIVEN that...'
column2: SIGNAL: the words 'given that', 'among', 'of those who'. | RULE: the condition becomes your new DENOMINATOR. Use only that row or column total, not the grand total. | This is the single most missed probability idea on the test.

column1: 16 PROB · M · Probability with percentages instead of counts
column2: MOVE: invent a convenient total, usually 100 or 1000, convert every percent to a count, then proceed as a normal table. | Makes the arithmetic concrete and removes the 'percent of a percent' confusion.

column1: 16 PROB · H · Expected value / 'how many would you expect'
column2: MOVE: probability x total = expected count. | If 26% of rooms have fewer than 18 seats and there are 50 rooms, expect 13. | Round only at the very end, and to a sensible whole number.

column1: 17 INFER · E · Reading a margin of error statement
column2: 'Estimated at $4.23 with a margin of error of $0.05' means the plausible range is $4.18 to $4.28. | MOVE: subtract and add the margin to get the interval. | The estimate is the CENTER of the interval.

column1: 17 INFER · E · Scaling a sample up to a population
column2: MOVE: sample proportion x population size. 16 of 20 employees is 0.8, so 0.8 x 400 = 320. | TRAP: use the proportion, not the raw sample count.

column1: 17 INFER · M · What makes a margin of error smaller
column2: RULE: a LARGER sample size shrinks the margin of error. Lower confidence level also shrinks it. | Nothing else on this test changes it. | TRAP: a bigger population does not shrink it; only a bigger sample does.

column1: 17 INFER · M · Who can you generalize to?
column2: RULE: conclusions apply ONLY to the population that was randomly sampled. | Sampled 30 Utah locations means you may conclude about Utah, not about the whole country. | Be wary of any choice that over-reaches the sampling frame.

column1: 17 INFER · H · SKIP-OK · Evaluating statistical claims
column2: This skill has only 12 items in the entire bank and 7 of them are Hard. | Lowest-yield topic on the math section. | If it appears: pick the most cautious, narrowest claim, and only say 'cause' if there was random ASSIGNMENT to groups.

column1: 18 AREA-VOL · E · 'Rectangle 64 by 32 inches. What is the area?'
column2: MOVE: A = length·width = 2,048 square inches. | TRAP: check whether they want area or PERIMETER (2l + 2w). The units tell you: square inches means area.

column1: 18 AREA-VOL · E · 'Side length of a square is 55 cm. Area in cm^2?'
column2: MOVE: A = s^2 = 3,025. | Square perimeter is 4s; square area is s^2. | TRAP: 4·55 = 220 is offered for people who grab perimeter.

column1: 18 AREA-VOL · E · 'Width is 7, length is 40 longer than the width. Find area.'
column2: SIGNAL: one dimension defined RELATIVE to the other. | MOVE: length = 7 + 40 = 47, then A = 7 x 47 = 329. | TRAP: using 40 as the length instead of 47. Translate the relationship first, then compute.

column1: 18 AREA-VOL · M · Composite and shaded-region figures
column2: MOVE: total area minus the removed piece. Name the two simple shapes before computing anything. | Write both areas down separately, then subtract. | TRAP: subtracting in the wrong order, or forgetting the removed shape appears twice.

column1: 18 AREA-VOL · M · Volume questions: pick the right solid
column2: MOVE: identify the solid, write the formula, substitute, then check units (cubic). | Most of these are one substitution once you have the formula. | The SAT gives a reference sheet, but looking it up costs 20 seconds you do not have.

column1: 18 AREA-VOL · M · Working backward from area or volume to a dimension
column2: SIGNAL: they give the volume and ask for a radius or height. | DESMOS: type the formula with the known value as an equation, e.g. 3.14x^2(10) = 500, and click the intersection. | Beats rearranging with cube roots by hand.

column1: 18 AREA-VOL · H · Scale changes in area and volume
column2: RULE: multiply every length by k and area scales by k^2, volume by k^3. | Tripling the radius multiplies volume by 27. | TRAP: the question gives a LENGTH ratio and asks for a VOLUME ratio. Cube it.

column1: 19 ANGLES · E · 'In triangle XYZ, angle X is 23 and angle Y is 66. Find angle Z.'
column2: RULE: the three angles of any triangle sum to 180. | MOVE: 180 - 23 - 66 = 91. | The most reliable easy point in geometry.

column1: 19 ANGLES · E · Two lines crossing, angles labeled w and z
column2: RULES: VERTICAL angles (opposite each other) are EQUAL. Angles on a straight line are SUPPLEMENTARY (sum 180). | Identify which relationship the picture shows, then write one equation.

column1: 19 ANGLES · E · Parallel lines cut by a transversal
column2: RULES: corresponding angles equal, alternate interior angles equal, same-side interior angles sum to 180. | SHORTCUT: every angle in the figure is either equal to the one you know or supplementary to it. Decide which by whether it looks acute or obtuse.

column1: 19 ANGLES · M · 'Figure not drawn to scale'
column2: WARNING: this phrase means you may NOT trust the picture's proportions or angle sizes. | Use only the stated measurements and the angle rules. | When it is absent, the figure IS roughly to scale and you can sanity-check by eye.

column1: 19 ANGLES · M · Similar triangles
column2: SIGNAL: 'DE is parallel to BC', nested triangles, or equal angle marks. | RULE: corresponding sides are PROPORTIONAL. Set up one ratio equation and solve. | Write the correspondence carefully: match the vertices in the same order.

column1: 19 ANGLES · M · Exterior angle and isosceles facts
column2: EXTERIOR angle = sum of the two remote interior angles. | ISOSCELES: equal sides sit opposite equal angles. | These two facts crack most 'find the missing angle' chains.

column1: 19 ANGLES · H · Multi-step angle chases
column2: MOVE: label EVERY angle you can deduce on the figure as you go, even ones you do not need yet. | The path is usually 3 or 4 short deductions, not one clever insight. | If you stall for 45 seconds, flag it and move.

column1: 20 RIGHT-TRI · E · Pythagorean theorem and the triples to memorize
column2: a^2 + b^2 = c^2, with c the hypotenuse (always opposite the right angle). | MEMORIZE: 3-4-5, 5-12-13, 8-15-17, 7-24-25, and all their multiples (6-8-10, 9-12-15). | Spotting a triple saves the whole computation.

column1: 20 RIGHT-TRI · E · SPECIAL RIGHT TRIANGLE: 45-45-90
column2: SIDES: x, x, x·sqrt(2). The hypotenuse is the leg times sqrt(2). | Appears as a square's diagonal or an isosceles right triangle. | Going backward: divide the hypotenuse by sqrt(2) to get a leg.

column1: 20 RIGHT-TRI · E · SPECIAL RIGHT TRIANGLE: 30-60-90
column2: SIDES: x (opposite 30), x·sqrt(3) (opposite 60), 2x (hypotenuse). | The short leg is always half the hypotenuse. | Appears as half of an equilateral triangle. Match the side to its OPPOSITE angle, not its position.

column1: 20 RIGHT-TRI · M · SOH CAH TOA
column2: sin = opposite/hypotenuse. cos = adjacent/hypotenuse. tan = opposite/adjacent. | MOVE: label the sides relative to the angle in question, then pick the ratio containing the two you care about. | SET DESMOS TO DEGREES first.

column1: 20 RIGHT-TRI · M · Given a trig ratio, find another side or ratio
column2: MOVE: sketch a right triangle, label the two sides the ratio gives you, use Pythagoras for the third, then read off whatever they ask. | sin = 3/5 means opposite 3, hypotenuse 5, so adjacent 4 and cos = 4/5.

column1: 20 RIGHT-TRI · M · Complementary angle identity
column2: RULE: sin(x) = cos(90 - x) and cos(x) = sin(90 - x). | So 'if sin(a) = 0.6 what is cos(90 - a)' answers itself: 0.6. | Recognizing this turns a hard-looking question into a one-second read.

column1: 20 RIGHT-TRI · H · SKIP-OK · Radians and the unit circle
column2: CONVERSION: 180 degrees = pi radians, so multiply by 180/pi to go to degrees. | Only 8 of 69 items in this skill are Easy, so this is a low-yield area for a 1300 target. | If it appears, convert to degrees and use Desmos in degree mode.

column1: 20 RIGHT-TRI · H · SKIP-OK · Trig in non-right triangles
column2: This requires laws of sines/cosines, which are outside the SAT's core. | If the triangle has no right angle and no special-triangle shape, flag and guess. | Spend that time re-checking your Algebra answers instead.

column1: 21 CIRCLE · E · Basic circle formulas
column2: AREA = pi·r^2. CIRCUMFERENCE = 2·pi·r = pi·d. | Diameter = 2r, so a diameter of 12.6 means a radius of 6.3. | TRAP: plugging the diameter into a formula that wants the radius. Halve it first, every time.

column1: 21 CIRCLE · E · Circle equation in standard form
column2: (x - h)^2 + (y - k)^2 = r^2 has CENTER (h, k) and RADIUS r. | For (x - 6)^2 + (y - 3)^2 = 81: center (6, 3), radius 9 (not 81). | TRAP: the signs flip, and the right side is r SQUARED. Take the square root.

column1: 21 CIRCLE · M · Circle equation in expanded form
column2: SIGNAL: x^2 + y^2 - 6x + 4y - 3 = 0, with no parentheses. | DESMOS: type it exactly as printed. Desmos graphs it, and you can read the center and radius off the picture. | This completely replaces completing the square twice.

column1: 21 CIRCLE · M · Arc length and sector area
column2: ARC LENGTH = (angle/360)·2·pi·r. SECTOR AREA = (angle/360)·pi·r^2. | Both are just the fraction of the full circle that the angle covers. | Write the fraction first, then multiply by the whole.

column1: 21 CIRCLE · H · SKIP-OK · Tangent lines and inscribed angles
column2: FACTS: a tangent is PERPENDICULAR to the radius at the point of contact, so its slope is the negative reciprocal of the radius's slope. An inscribed angle is HALF its intercepted arc. | Only 4 of 67 circle items are Easy, so this is a flag-and-guess zone at a 1300 target.

column1: 21 CIRCLE · H · SKIP-OK · Central-angle triangles inside a circle
column2: SIGNAL: 'center O, points R and S on the circle, angle ROS = 88, find angle RSO.' | KEY: two radii make the triangle ISOSCELES, so the two base angles are equal: (180 - 88)/2 = 46. | Worth knowing because it turns an intimidating question into simple arithmetic.

column1: 22 FORMULAS · Area
column2: Rectangle: l·w. Square: s^2. Triangle: (1/2)·b·h. Parallelogram: b·h. Trapezoid: (1/2)·(b1 + b2)·h. Circle: pi·r^2. | Height must be PERPENDICULAR to the base, not a slanted side.

column1: 22 FORMULAS · Volume
column2: Rectangular prism: l·w·h. Cylinder: pi·r^2·h. Sphere: (4/3)·pi·r^3. Cone: (1/3)·pi·r^2·h. Pyramid: (1/3)·B·h, where B is the base area. | The cone and pyramid both carry the 1/3; the cylinder and prism do not.

column1: 22 FORMULAS · Surface area
column2: Sphere: 4·pi·r^2. Cylinder (total): 2·pi·r^2 + 2·pi·r·h. Rectangular prism: 2·(lw + lh + wh). | Surface area is in SQUARE units; volume is in CUBIC units. Units alone often tell you which they want.

column1: 22 FORMULAS · Special right triangles
column2: 45-45-90: x, x, x·sqrt(2). | 30-60-90: x, x·sqrt(3), 2x with x opposite the 30-degree angle. | Triples: 3-4-5, 5-12-13, 8-15-17, 7-24-25.

column1: 22 FORMULAS · Linear equation formats
column2: SLOPE-INTERCEPT: y = mx + b (m slope, b y-intercept). | POINT-SLOPE: y - y1 = m(x - x1). | STANDARD: Ax + By = C, with slope -A/B and y-intercept C/B. | Slope between two points: (y2 - y1)/(x2 - x1).

column1: 22 FORMULAS · Nonlinear equation formats
column2: QUADRATIC STANDARD: y = ax^2 + bx + c (c is the y-intercept). | FACTORED: y = a(x - r)(x - s) (r and s are the roots). | VERTEX: y = a(x - h)^2 + k (vertex at (h, k)). | EXPONENTIAL: y = A·b^(t/p). | CIRCLE: (x - h)^2 + (y - k)^2 = r^2.

column1: 22 FORMULAS · Quadratic essentials
column2: QUADRATIC FORMULA: x = (-b ± sqrt(b^2 - 4ac))/(2a). | VERTEX x-coordinate: -b/(2a). | DISCRIMINANT b^2 - 4ac: positive = 2 real roots, zero = 1, negative = 0. | Sum of roots = -b/a, product = c/a.

column1: 22 FORMULAS · Growth and decay rates
column2: EXPONENTIAL: y = A·b^(t/p). Growth of r percent: b = 1 + r/100. Decay of r percent: b = 1 - r/100. | Doubling b = 2, halving b = 1/2, tripling b = 3. | LINEAR growth adds a fixed amount; EXPONENTIAL multiplies by a fixed factor.

column1: 22 FORMULAS · Coordinate geometry
column2: DISTANCE: sqrt((x2-x1)^2 + (y2-y1)^2). | MIDPOINT: ((x1+x2)/2, (y1+y2)/2). | Parallel means equal slopes; perpendicular means slopes multiply to -1. | DESMOS: distance((1,2),(4,6)) computes it directly.

column1: 22 FORMULAS · Percent and statistics
column2: Percent change: ((new - old)/old)·100. Part = percent·whole. | Successive changes MULTIPLY their factors. | Mean = sum/count; work with TOTALS when a mean changes. | Scale factor k: area x k^2, volume x k^3.

column1: 22 FORMULAS · Angle facts
column2: Triangle angles sum to 180; quadrilateral to 360. | Vertical angles equal; straight line supplementary (180). | Parallel lines: corresponding and alternate interior angles equal, same-side interior sum 180. | Exterior angle = sum of remote interior angles. | 180 degrees = pi radians.
